newsitem.title: USA: Firmer dlr only mild palliative for ailing Europe.
newsitem.headline: Firmer dlr only mild palliative for ailing Europe.

text.p: A rapidly appreciating dollar should offer marginal relief to plodding European economies that are banking on export-led growth in the run-up to European monetary union.
But this relief may not manifest itself fully until late 1997 and even then, the impact on overall growth numbers is unlikely to be significant, economists said this week.
"On the margins it's helpful for them, but we're really talking about basis points of growth and not percentage points," said Ron Leven, currency strategist at J.P. Morgan.

"Trade flows are far more sensitive to relative economic activity than they are to exchange rate movements," he added, characterizing the trade impact of currency fluctuations as "modest and drawn out."
The dollar's ascension to two-and-a-half year highs against both the German mark and the French franc has gained impressive momentum in recent weeks.
Since the beginning of the year, the dollar has risen some 10 pfennigs against the mark compared to roughly 12 pfennigs in all of 1996.
The greenback's 35 centimes climb against the French franc in the first three weeks of 1997 matches its total gains for the previous year.

Underscoring the enthusiastic European response to recent dollar gains, Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said on Wednesday that the dollar's rise offered the "only ray of light" for German economic growth.
But whether this light promises much in the way of a near-term reprieve from Germany's fundamental growth problems and high unemployment is doubtful, experts said.

"We probably will see stronger economic numbers coming out of Europe, but I don't think we're going to see much in the first or second quarters," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc.

"The export sectors will look better and that will feed through to improved business confidence but 1997 is a year in which growth is not going to be strong enough to bring about a reversal of the trends in unemployment in Europe," he added.
Although the lion's share of European trade is concentrated within Europe itself, economists said there were clear trade benefits to be had from the stronger dollar.

Since a substantial portion of Europe's exports to other parts of the world, and some within Europe, are dollar based, big exporters such as European planemaking consortium Airbus Industrie and German automaker Daimler-Benz AG can take bigger mark-ups or make prices more competitive as a result of the stronger dollar.

But even as analysts increase their expectations for export growth in countries such as France and Germany, they remain skeptical about overall growth prospects given a glaring lack of domestic demand.
Analysts said that Europe has looked favorably upon a robust dollar and is likely to continue to do so due to other reasons besides its implications for exporters.

A stronger dollar is welcome in Europe, J.P. Morgan's Leven said, because it could delay an interest rate tightening by the Fed. He said a U.S. rate hike could signal a more generalized trend toward global tightening and choke off U.S. demand for foreign goods -- both negatives for Europe.
He also noted that weaker European currencies, on the margins, could stem the tide of European manufacturers that are moving production overseas.
"There's a general level of concern in Europe that strong currencies will abet this process of movement of industry outside of Europe," said Leven.
Welteke's comments on Wednesday highlighted the hopes that a stronger dollar generates within countries struggling down the road toward EMU.
But U.S. experts believe Europe's economic problems are bound to continue in the months ahead regardless of exchange rate fluctuations.

"Just as the European central banks want to argue that European interest rates are low enough to fuel growth, I would argue the same thing is true about foreign exchange rates," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "Current currency prices are consistent with stronger growth, but European problems are much deeper than prices."
((-- N.A. Treasury Desk 212-859-1673))
